subject: health
unitTitle: Body Systems, Hygiene, and Disease Prevention
title: Application or project: oral health
essentialQuestion: How can understanding body systems, hygiene, and disease prevention help us explain, decide, create, or solve something that matters?
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible response tool
the fictional lesson cards included in this task
keyPoints: Oral care removes plaque from teeth and along the gumline; brushing, cleaning between teeth, and routine dental care protect function as well as comfort.
Compare care options by function, access, safety, and sustainability; avoid appearance rules, shame, rigid perfection, or assumptions about another person’s habits.
For oral health, a strong response distinguishes fact from assumption, uses a fictional or public case, and includes a safe next step or appropriate source of support.
privacySafeScenario: All required evidence uses fictional or public situations. The learner never has to disclose personal health, body, treatment, feelings, family, sexual, or substance-use information.
studentTask: Write two facts. Use the lesson idea about oral health. Choose one safe next step. Name an adult or help source.
knowledgeCheck: Name the fact. Fix the wrong claim. Choose a safe action. Name who can help.
completionCriteria: I choose a safe action and give a reason.
I name the right kind of help.
adaptationChoices: Show one short direction at a time. Allow reading aloud, word cards, typing, writing, drawing with labels, signing, selecting, or speaking. Help may repeat a direction but may not choose the fact, action, reason, or help source.
extensionChallenge: Create a new fictional or public case about oral health. Include enough facts, choices or constraints, and support authority for another learner to reason safely. Add an accurate explanation of acceptable variation; use no real person's private information.
accessibilitySupports: Show one action at a time.
Offer a vocabulary card and extra time.
Accept typing, writing, drawing with labels, signing, selecting, or speaking for equal credit.
trustedAdultNote: If a real situation feels unsafe or raises a health concern, pause the lesson and tell a parent, guardian, teacher, school staff member, or another trusted adult. A qualified health professional gives medical advice. In an emergency, get an adult and use the local emergency service.

optionalReflection.prompt: Optional and private: Make up one example that helps you remember oral health. Keep it for yourself. You do not need to show it or prove that you completed it.

neverRequires: This task never requires body weight, height, BMI, body-fat percentage, body comparison, or appearance scoring.
This task never requires calorie counting, dieting, or a diet or weight-loss goal.
This task never requires sharing medical history, a diagnosis, treatment, medication, feelings, family conflict, or sexual history.
This task never requires a photograph, video, or voice recording of the learner as proof.
This task never requires a public performance or an audience.
This task never requires advice about an individual learner's treatment, medication, food, supplement, or exercise plan.

contentProvenance.objective: Create, test, or revise a meaningful product that applies oral health and the unit standards.

learningGoal: I can explain oral health, use facts, choose a safe next step, and name who can help.

lessonExperience.privacyNotice: Write only about the made-up people. Keep private information private.

entryCheck.heading: Start with a fact

choices: Oral care removes plaque from teeth and along the gumline; brushing, cleaning between teeth, and routine dental care protect function as well as comfort.

entryCheck.support: A fact is stated in the lesson or supported by reliable evidence. An assumption adds a conclusion the information cannot establish.
entryCheck.treatment: This entry check is unscored. Use the support or prerequisite route before continuing when needed.

vocabularyCheck.heading: Check the words
vocabularyCheck.selfCheck: A complete check uses the meaning of oral health, one accurate fact, and the responsible support route without labeling a person.

modelExample.heading: Watch the reasoning: oral health
modelExample.situation: A fictional Northside youth council is designing a public resource about oral health. It has this approved evidence: Oral care removes plaque from teeth and along the gumline; brushing, cleaning between teeth, and routine dental care protect function as well as comfort. The resource must name its audience, a feasible action, the actor with authority, an access or privacy safeguard, and a measure of impact.
relevantFacts: Oral care removes plaque from teeth and along the gumline; brushing, cleaning between teeth, and routine dental care protect function as well as comfort.
Compare care options by function, access, safety, and sustainability; avoid appearance rules, shame, rigid perfection, or assumptions about another person’s habits.
modelExample.assumptionOrDistraction: A popular or confident statement about oral health is not automatically accurate and cannot establish a person's health, motives, or character.
possibleActions: Build the bounded public resource with evidence, authority, safeguards, and a measure.
Require a real personal health plan.
Publish a claim without checking evidence or access.
modelExample.successCheck: The model uses the lesson fact, explains the connection, stays within the learner role, and names responsible help when it is needed.
workedReasoning: Define one bounded fictional or public need and the audience affected.
Use the lesson fact, identify the actor with authority, and propose a feasible response.
Add an access or privacy safeguard and a measure that could show whether the response worked.

guidedReasoning.heading: Try a different case with support
guidedReasoning.situation: A fictional Riverside youth group must explain or act on oral health. The group has this reliable lesson information: Compare care options by function, access, safety, and sustainability; avoid appearance rules, shame, rigid perfection, or assumptions about another person’s habits. It has not been given any person's private health information.
availableChoices: Use the stated facts and compare safe options.
Pause and contact the responsible help source.
turnOne: Name an adult who can help.
guidedReasoning.cue: Look for the situation, safe choices, relevant information, and who can help.
feedbackMoves: If a response adds a guess, replace it with a fact from the case or lesson.
If oral health is named without explanation, link one fact to the concept or process.
If a choice is reasonable but the reason is missing, add the fact that supports it.
If a response seeks disclosure, diagnoses, shames, or exceeds the learner role, switch to the fictional facts and the approved help route.
Accept an equivalent typed, handwritten, drawn-and-labeled, signed, selected, or spoken response when it shows the same reasoning.
guidedReasoning.turnTwo: Fix one sentence. Use a fact and a safe next step.
guidedReasoning.releaseCondition: Continue when the response uses a stated fact, applies oral health, and gives a safe next step without private disclosure or a person label.

independentEvidence.heading: Show what you know on a fresh case
independentEvidence.situation: A fictional Maple Community Center requests a bounded public resource about oral health. Use this evidence: Oral care removes plaque from teeth and along the gumline; brushing, cleaning between teeth, and routine dental care protect function as well as comfort. Define the audience and need, propose a feasible action, identify authority, add an access or privacy safeguard, and define a measure.
directions: Use the lesson idea about oral health.
Name an adult or help source.
permittedSupports: read-aloud or one direction at a time
typing, writing, drawing with labels, signing, selecting, or speaking
independentEvidence.independenceBoundary: Support may restate a direction or provide access. It may not choose the controlling fact, conclusion, action, reason, safety judgment, or help route.
successCriteria: I choose a safe action and give a reason.
I name the right kind of help.

freshMasteryCheck.heading: Check the idea in a new place
freshMasteryCheck.situation: A fictional Lakeside school committee reviews oral health. The committee knows: For oral health, a strong response distinguishes fact from assumption, uses a fictional or public case, and includes a safe next step or appropriate source of support. It must correct one unsupported claim and choose a safe next step.
freshMasteryCheck.freshnessNote: This case is different from the model, guided case, and independent case. Do not copy their conclusions.

remediation.heading: Try a different model
remediation.trigger: Use this route after an observable gap in a fact, vocabulary meaning, reasoning step, process order, or help route for oral health.
remediation.prerequisite: First restate this approved fact in your own words: Oral care removes plaque from teeth and along the gumline; brushing, cleaning between teeth, and routine dental care protect function as well as comfort.
remediation.alternateExplanation: Use a bridge diagram: NEED and EVIDENCE are one side; ACTION, AUTHORITY, SAFEGUARD, and MEASURE are the spans. A proposal cannot cross the bridge when one span is missing.
contrast: Sufficient: uses a stated fact about oral health, explains the connection, and stays within the learner role.
Needs revision: repeats a topic word, adds a guess, or gives an action with no factual reason or responsible help source.
remediation.guidedCorrection: Cross out the guess. Circle the fact. Add one safe action.

freshRetry.situation: A fictional Oak Street library receives a new question about oral health. Staff provide this approved fact: Compare care options by function, access, safety, and sustainability; avoid appearance rules, shame, rigid perfection, or assumptions about another person’s habits. The learner must respond without using the Northside, Riverside, Maple, or Lakeside conclusions.

remediation.exitCriterion: Return to the independent route when the learner accurately uses a fact, applies oral health, explains a safe response, and identifies support without answer-bearing help.
remediation.nextRoute: If the same gap remains, return to the named prerequisite with an adult instructor; do not replace the task with private reflection.

laterTransfer.timing: Use in a later lesson or a separate session.
laterTransfer.prompt: Apply oral health to a meaningfully different fictional or public case. Retrieve the concept, use relevant facts, justify a safe response, and identify the responsible support or authority route.
laterTransfer.masteryBoundary: The current independent response is one evidence occasion. Mastery requires accurate independent evidence now and accurate later retrieval or transfer.
